learn.hook: You pull your hand off a hot tawa before you even 'think' about it — your spinal cord took that decision!
points: Receptors in sense organs detect information — e.g. taste receptors (gustatory) on the tongue and smell receptors (olfactory) in the nose.

A neuron has dendrites (pick up information), a cell body, and a long axon. The message travels as an electrical impulse from dendrite → cell body → axon; at the axon end chemicals are released that cross the gap (synapse) to the next cell.

Reflex action: a quick, automatic response, e.g. withdrawing a hand from a flame. Path (reflex arc): receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron in spinal cord → motor neuron → effector muscle. The message also reaches the brain.

Brain: the forebrain is the main thinking part, with areas for hearing, smell and sight and for controlling voluntary muscles. The hindbrain's medulla controls involuntary actions like blood pressure, salivation and vomiting; the cerebellum keeps balance and posture and makes voluntary actions precise.

The brain is protected by the skull and a fluid-filled cushion; the spinal cord by the vertebral column. Muscles move because their cells contain special proteins that change shape and arrangement when a nerve impulse arrives.

example.q: Think it through: you are riding a bicycle on a narrow lane and keep your balance. Which part of the brain is busiest?
steps: Balance and posture are maintained by the cerebellum.
The cerebellum also makes voluntary movements precise, like steering.
So it is constantly adjusting your body on the cycle.

learn.reallife: When the doctor taps just below your knee and your leg kicks up, she is testing a reflex arc that runs through your spinal cord.

games.title: A reflex arc in action
items: Receptor in the skin senses heat
Sensory neuron carries the impulse
Relay neuron in the spinal cord
Motor neuron carries the command
Arm muscle (effector) pulls the hand away

games.title: Match the brain part to its job
pairs: Thinking, and areas for sight, hearing and smell
Site where many reflex arcs are formed

quiz.q: In which direction does an impulse travel through a neuron?
quiz.explain: Dendrites pick up the information, it passes through the cell body and travels along the axon to its end.
steps: Dendrites pick up information first.
The message then passes through the cell body.
It travels along the axon to its end.
So the direction is dendrite → cell body → axon.
Answer: Dendrite → cell body → axon
quiz.mistake: Reverses the direction of the impulse

quiz.q: What is a synapse?
options: The gap between the end of one neuron and the next cell
The cell body of a neuron
quiz.explain: At the synapse, chemicals released from the axon end carry the message across to the next neuron or a muscle.
steps: At the end of an axon there is a small gap before the next cell.
Chemicals released from the axon end cross this gap.
The gap is called the synapse.
Answer: The gap between the end of one neuron and the next cell
quiz.mistake: Thinks neurons physically touch each other

quiz.q: Where are reflex arcs mostly formed?
quiz.explain: Reflex arcs are formed in the spinal cord so the response is quick, though the brain also receives the information.
steps: A reflex must be very quick.
So the reflex arc is formed in the spinal cord, without waiting for the brain.
The brain still receives the information.
So reflex arcs are mostly formed in the spinal cord.
Answer: In the spinal cord
quiz.mistake: Thinks every response must be decided by the brain

quiz.q: Which part of the brain controls involuntary actions like salivation and vomiting?
quiz.explain: The medulla in the hindbrain controls such involuntary actions, along with blood pressure.
steps: Involuntary actions like salivation, vomiting and blood pressure are controlled by the hindbrain.
The part responsible is the medulla.
The cerebellum controls balance and precision.
So the answer is the medulla.
Answer: Medulla
quiz.mistake: Mixes up medulla and cerebellum

quiz.q: Picking up a pencil accurately depends mainly on the —
quiz.explain: The cerebellum makes voluntary actions precise and helps maintain posture and balance.
steps: Picking up a pencil accurately is a precise voluntary action.
The cerebellum makes voluntary actions precise and keeps balance and posture.
So it depends mainly on the cerebellum.
Answer: Cerebellum
quiz.mistake: Thinks the medulla controls voluntary actions

quiz.q: How do muscle cells shorten when they receive a nerve impulse?
options: Special proteins in them change shape and arrangement
quiz.explain: Muscle cells contain proteins that change their shape and arrangement, making the cell shorter.
steps: Muscle cells contain special proteins.
When an impulse arrives, these proteins change their shape and arrangement.
This makes the muscle cell shorter.
Answer: Special proteins in them change shape and arrangement
quiz.mistake: Confuses muscle movement with plant cell water movement

quiz.q: Which part of the neuron acquires information from the surroundings?
quiz.explain: Dendrite tips pick up information and set off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse.
steps: The dendrite tips pick up information.
This sets off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse.
The axon carries the impulse away.
So the dendrite acquires information.
Answer: Dendrite
quiz.mistake: Thinks the axon receives the message

quiz.q: How is the brain protected inside the body?
options: By the skull and a fluid-filled cushion around it
quiz.explain: The brain sits in the bony skull, cushioned by fluid that absorbs shocks.
steps: The brain sits inside the bony skull.
A fluid-filled cushion around it absorbs shocks.
The vertebral column protects the spinal cord, not the brain.
So the brain is protected by the skull and a fluid-filled cushion.
Answer: By the skull and a fluid-filled cushion around it
quiz.mistake: Mixes up protection of the brain and the spinal cord

teach.ask: Gappu touched a hot chai cup: 'My wing jumped back before I even thought! How did that happen?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The sensory neuron told the spinal cord, and the motor neuron pulled my wing back — a reflex!
teach.nudge: Close! Which part — brain or spinal cord — handled that quick response?

revise.summary: The nervous system carries messages as electrical impulses through neurons, from dendrite to cell body to axon, crossing synapses chemically. Reflex arcs in the spinal cord give quick responses, and the brain controls thinking, involuntary actions and balance.
focus: Trace the path of an impulse through a neuron and across a synapse
Draw the reflex arc: receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron → motor neuron → effector
Match brain parts to their jobs: forebrain, medulla, cerebellum
remember: Impulse direction: dendrite → cell body → axon
Reflex arcs are mostly formed in the spinal cord
Medulla: involuntary actions (blood pressure, salivation, vomiting); cerebellum: balance and precise voluntary actions
Brain is protected by the skull and a fluid-filled cushion; spinal cord by the vertebral column
traps: Don't reverse the impulse direction (it never starts at the axon)
The synapse is a gap, not a part of the cell body
The cerebellum, not the medulla, controls balance and posture

learn.hook: Your body has a postal service: tiny glands send chemical letters called hormones through your blood!
points: Hormones are chemical messengers made by endocrine glands and released directly into the blood, so they reach cells all over the body.
Adrenaline (adrenal glands) prepares the body for an emergency: the heart beats faster, more blood goes to skeletal muscles and breathing becomes faster.
Thyroxine (thyroid) controls carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism. Making it needs iodine; lack of iodine can cause goitre (swollen neck), which is why we use iodised salt.

Growth hormone (pituitary) controls growth; its deficiency in childhood causes dwarfism. The hypothalamus releases a releasing factor that makes the pituitary secrete growth hormone. Testosterone (testes) and oestrogen (ovaries) bring about changes at puberty.

Insulin (pancreas) controls blood sugar; too little causes diabetes. Hormones work by feedback: when blood sugar rises, pancreatic cells detect it and release more insulin; when it falls, less is released.

example.q: Think it through: a stray dog suddenly barks and chases you. Your heart pounds and you run faster than ever. Which hormone did this?
steps: Emergencies trigger the adrenal glands.
They release adrenaline into the blood.
Adrenaline speeds up the heart and sends more blood and oxygen to muscles, preparing you to run.

learn.reallife: The 'iodised' label on your salt packet is there because iodine helps the thyroid make thyroxine and prevents goitre.

games.title: Match the hormone to its gland
Hormone facts
items: Hormones travel to their target cells through the blood.
Endocrine glands release hormones directly into blood.
Iodine is needed to make thyroxine.
Lack of iodine can cause goitre.
Insulin raises the level of sugar in the blood.
Insulin helps lower and regulate blood sugar.
Deficiency of growth hormone in childhood causes dwarfism.
Growth hormone from the pituitary controls growth.
The timing and amount of hormone release are controlled by feedback mechanisms.
E.g. rising blood sugar triggers more insulin release.
Adrenaline slows down the heartbeat in an emergency.
It makes the heart beat faster to supply more oxygen.

quiz.q: Which hormone prepares the body to face an emergency?
quiz.explain: Adrenaline from the adrenal glands speeds up heartbeat and breathing and diverts blood to muscles.
steps: Adrenaline from the adrenal glands is released in an emergency.
It speeds up heartbeat and breathing and sends more blood to the muscles.
So adrenaline prepares the body to face an emergency.
Answer: Adrenaline
quiz.mistake: Thinks thyroxine controls emergencies

quiz.q: Which mineral is needed by the thyroid gland to make thyroxine?
quiz.explain: Thyroxine contains iodine, so iodine deficiency can cause goitre.
steps: The thyroid gland makes thyroxine.
Thyroxine contains iodine, so iodine is needed.
Lack of iodine causes goitre (hence iodised salt).
So the mineral is iodine.
Answer: Iodine
quiz.mistake: Confuses iodine with iron needed for haemoglobin

quiz.q: A person whose pancreas produces too little insulin is likely to have —
quiz.explain: Insulin regulates blood sugar; too little insulin raises blood sugar, causing diabetes.
steps: Insulin from the pancreas controls blood sugar.
Too little insulin lets blood sugar rise.
This condition is diabetes.
Answer: Diabetes
quiz.mistake: Links insulin to the wrong disorder

quiz.q: Which gland secretes growth hormone?
quiz.explain: The pituitary gland secretes growth hormone, controlled by a releasing factor from the hypothalamus.
steps: Growth hormone controls growth.
It is secreted by the pituitary gland.
The hypothalamus sends a releasing factor that makes the pituitary release it.
So the gland is the pituitary.
Answer: Pituitary
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the pituitary and the thyroid

quiz.q: How do hormones reach their target organs?
quiz.explain: Endocrine glands have no ducts; hormones are released directly into blood, which carries them around the body.
steps: Endocrine glands have no ducts.
They release hormones directly into the blood.
The blood carries them to cells all over the body.
So hormones reach target organs through the blood.
Answer: Through the blood
quiz.mistake: Confuses hormonal and nervous signals

quiz.q: Which hormone is responsible for changes in boys at puberty, like a deeper voice?
quiz.explain: Testosterone from the testes brings about male puberty changes.
steps: Testosterone is made by the testes.
It brings about changes in boys at puberty, such as a deeper voice.
Oestrogen does this for girls.
So the hormone is testosterone.
Answer: Testosterone
quiz.mistake: Swaps the male and female hormones

quiz.q: Which is an example of a feedback mechanism?
options: Pulling a hand away from a flame
Rising blood sugar causing more insulin to be released
quiz.explain: The result (high sugar) controls the release of insulin, which in turn brings the sugar down.
steps: In a feedback mechanism, the result controls how much hormone is released.
Rising blood sugar is detected by the pancreas, which releases more insulin.
The insulin then brings sugar down.
So this is a feedback mechanism: rising blood sugar causing more insulin release.
Answer: Rising blood sugar causing more insulin to be released
quiz.mistake: Confuses feedback with reflex action

quiz.q: What is the job of the hypothalamus in growth?
options: It releases a factor that stimulates the pituitary to secrete growth hormone
quiz.explain: The hypothalamus sends a releasing factor to the pituitary, which then releases growth hormone.
steps: The hypothalamus releases a releasing factor.
This factor makes the pituitary secrete growth hormone.
So it stimulates the pituitary to secrete growth hormone.
Answer: It releases a factor that stimulates the pituitary to secrete growth hormone
quiz.mistake: Thinks the hypothalamus itself makes growth hormone

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does my heart thump when a cat appears? Who sends that message?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The adrenal gland sends adrenaline through the blood and my heart beats faster to escape!
teach.nudge: Good! But how does the hormone travel from the gland to the heart?

revise.summary: Hormones are chemical messengers from endocrine glands, released into the blood. Adrenaline, thyroxine, growth hormone, testosterone, oestrogen and insulin control emergencies, metabolism, growth, puberty and blood sugar, often through feedback.
focus: Match each hormone to its gland and job
Know the deficiency effects: goitre, dwarfism, diabetes
Explain feedback control using insulin and blood sugar
remember: Thyroxine (thyroid) needs iodine; iodine deficiency causes goitre
Growth hormone from the pituitary, triggered by a releasing factor from the hypothalamus
Insulin (pancreas) controls blood sugar; too little causes diabetes
traps: Hormones travel in blood, not along nerves
Goitre is due to lack of iodine, not lack of insulin
Testosterone is from the testes; oestrogen is from the ovaries

learn.hook: Plants have no nerves, yet a chhui-mui leaf folds when you touch it and sunflowers chase the light!
points: Plants respond without nerves. Touch-me-not (Mimosa pudica, chhui-mui) folds its leaves quickly by changing the amount of water in its cells — no growth is involved.

Tropisms are slow, growth-related movements towards or away from a stimulus: phototropism (light — shoots bend towards it), geotropism (gravity — roots grow down), hydrotropism (water) and chemotropism (chemicals, e.g. pollen tubes growing towards ovules).
Tendrils of a pea plant coil around a support because the part of the tendril away from the object grows faster than the part touching it.
Auxin is made at the shoot tip. When light comes from one side, auxin moves to the shady side, those cells grow longer, and the shoot bends towards light.
Gibberellins help stems grow; cytokinins promote cell division and are found in fruits and seeds; abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves.

example.q: Think it through: a potted money plant on a window sill gradually bends towards the window. Explain.
steps: Light falls on the shoot from one side.
Auxin collects on the shaded side of the shoot.
Cells on the shaded side grow longer than those on the lit side.
Unequal growth bends the shoot towards light — positive phototropism.
example.answer: Auxin makes cells on the shaded side grow longer, so the shoot bends towards the light.

learn.reallife: Gardeners turn their pots every few days so plants on a balcony grow straight instead of leaning towards the light.

games.title: Which type of plant movement?
items: Shoot bending towards light
Roots growing downward
Pollen tube growing towards the ovule
Pea tendril coiling around a stick
Chhui-mui leaves folding when touched
Roots growing towards water

items.text: The hormone made at the shoot tip that makes cells grow longer is ___.
___ promote cell division and are found in fruits and seeds.
The hormone that inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves is ___ acid.
Roots grow downward in response to gravity. This is ___.
___ help in the growth of the stem.

quiz.q: How do the leaves of the touch-me-not plant fold when touched?
options: By rapid growth of new cells
By changing the amount of water in their cells
quiz.explain: Cells change shape by gaining or losing water; no growth is involved, which is why the movement is quick.
steps: Touch-me-not leaves fold quickly when touched.
The cells change shape by changing the amount of water in them.
No growth is involved, so the movement is fast.
So they fold by changing the amount of water in their cells.
Answer: By changing the amount of water in their cells
quiz.mistake: Thinks every plant movement is due to growth

quiz.q: The growth of a pollen tube towards the ovule is an example of —
quiz.explain: The pollen tube grows in response to chemicals released near the ovule.
steps: The pollen tube grows towards chemicals released near the ovule.
Growth in response to chemicals is chemotropism.
So it is chemotropism.
Answer: Chemotropism
quiz.mistake: Confuses chemical stimulus with water or light

quiz.q: Why does a shoot bend towards light coming from one side?
options: Auxin collects on the lit side and shortens cells there
Light kills cells on the bright side
Auxin collects on the shaded side, making those cells grow longer
The shoot is pulled by sunlight
quiz.explain: More auxin on the shady side causes more elongation there, so the shoot curves towards light.
steps: Auxin is made at the shoot tip.
With light from one side, auxin moves to the shaded side.
Cells on the shaded side grow longer, so the shoot bends towards light.
So auxin collects on the shaded side, making those cells grow longer.
Answer: Auxin collects on the shaded side, making those cells grow longer
quiz.mistake: Puts auxin on the wrong side

quiz.q: Which plant hormone inhibits growth?
quiz.explain: Abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves; the other three promote growth.
steps: Auxin, gibberellins and cytokinins promote growth.
Abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves.
So the growth-inhibiting hormone is abscisic acid.
Answer: Abscisic acid
quiz.mistake: Thinks all plant hormones promote growth

quiz.q: Roots grow towards the earth. This is —
quiz.explain: Growth in the direction of gravity is positive geotropism.
steps: Roots grow downwards, in the direction of gravity.
Movement in response to gravity is geotropism.
Growth towards the stimulus is positive.
So it is positive geotropism.
Answer: Positive geotropism
quiz.mistake: Mixes up positive and negative tropism

quiz.q: How does a pea tendril wind around a support?
options: The part touching the support grows faster
The part away from the support grows faster
It changes water content within seconds
quiz.explain: Faster growth on the outer side (away from the support) makes the tendril coil around it.
steps: The tendril touches the support on one side.
The part away from the support grows faster than the part touching it.
This uneven growth makes the tendril coil around the support.
Answer: The part away from the support grows faster
quiz.mistake: Reverses which side grows faster

quiz.q: Cytokinins are present in high concentration in —
options: Areas of rapid cell division such as fruits and seeds
quiz.explain: Cytokinins promote cell division and are found where cells divide rapidly.
steps: Cytokinins promote cell division.
So they are found where cells divide rapidly.
Fruits and seeds are such areas.
So cytokinins are high in areas of rapid cell division such as fruits and seeds.
Answer: Areas of rapid cell division such as fruits and seeds
quiz.mistake: Confuses cytokinins with abscisic acid

quiz.q: Which is the main difference between control in plants and in animals?
options: Plants use hormones and changes in cell water content, not nerves and muscles
quiz.explain: Plants lack nervous tissue and muscles; they coordinate through plant hormones and cell changes.
steps: Animals use nerves and muscles for control.
Plants have no nervous tissue or muscles.
They coordinate using plant hormones and changes in cell water content.
Answer: Plants use hormones and changes in cell water content, not nerves and muscles
quiz.mistake: Thinks plants have nerves

teach.ask: Gappu sees a plant on the windowsill: 'Why is it leaning towards the window? Does it have eyes?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Auxin moves to the shady side, those cells grow longer, and the shoot bends to the light!
teach.nudge: Good! But which side of the shoot grows faster, and which hormone makes it do so?

revise.summary: Plants respond without nerves. Touch-me-not moves quickly by changing cell water content, while tropisms are slow growth movements towards or away from light, gravity, water or chemicals, controlled by plant hormones.
focus: Tell quick non-growth movements (touch-me-not) from growth movements (tropisms)
Name and give examples of phototropism, geotropism, hydrotropism and chemotropism
Know the roles of auxin, gibberellins, cytokinins and abscisic acid
remember: Auxin moves to the shaded side, making those cells longer, so shoots bend towards light
Roots show positive geotropism; pollen tubes show chemotropism
Pea tendrils coil because the side away from the support grows faster
Abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes wilting; cytokinins promote cell division
traps: Touch-me-not's folding is not growth; it is a change in cell water content
Auxin collects on the shaded side, not the lit side
Abscisic acid inhibits growth; the other three hormones promote it
